description: Where the debugged game is stopped: the stack trace, what is in scope at a frame with the values, or the debugger's console output so far, its last thousand lines, with any earlier ones counted under notShown. For a game this server started the output is what the game printed. The errors and warnings it reported, with where each happened, are in editor_output, which also has what it printed once it has ended, as its debugger ends with it. For a game this server started, its keeper's debugger answers: each frame names its script as the project spells it under script and on this machine under path, and held says which thread stopped and why. For a game the editor plays, the editor's debug adapter answers. A stop is reported by the editor's adapter only to the sessions connected when it happened, so a server that connected afterwards, which is every server after a reconnect, is shown a thread and no frames about a game still sitting at its breakpoint. That server asks the runtime instead: a held game accepts a connection and never answers, and the refusal then says held rather than running, and that the stack cannot be read from here. debug_control continue lets it go, and the next stop is one this session is told about, with its stack. A function that awaited is resumed with no caller below it, since the call that started it returned at the await, so its frame is the only one. A value inside an array or a dictionary is shown as the engine prints it: a String quoted, a StringName as &"name", a NodePath as ^"path" and a whole float with .0. In a game this server started, a typed array or dictionary is typed as declared, such as Array[String], and a list or a dictionary shows its first 20 entries and says how many more it holds. An evaluate such as items.slice(20, 40) reads the rest. Members lists the script's variables and not its constants, which an evaluate reads by name. The variables give an object as its class and instance id only, and evaluate reads into it: an expression worked out by the game at a frame, with the frame's locals, the globals and every global class in scope and the frame's instance as self, such as wave.spawned or wave.spawned.size(). The game runs what the expression calls, so a call that changes something changes the game. A frame with no instance, a static function's called on its class, is refused, since the engine lets the game go on rather than evaluate there. The frame below it has one. The compiler's own locals, named with @ such as a for loop's @counter_pos, are left out. Operations: stack: the stack trace; variables: locals, members and globals at a frame, with their values; evaluate (needs expression): what an expression comes to at a frame, worked out by the held game; output: console output captured through the debug adapter. Default stack.

expression.description: evaluate: a GDScript expression, as Godot's Expression class parses it: members of self by name, locals, autoloads and global classes, operators, indexing and calls, such as wave.spawned[0] or Ledger.entries.size(). An expression that does not parse, or fails as it runs, comes to null with failed saying why, as the engine words it, and a null with no failed is the value. The error the engine prints for it is in the run's output as info with raisedBy debug_state evaluate, and does not count among the run's errors. The engine loads every global class's script for the first evaluate of a run, so the errors of one that does not parse are the evaluate's too. After that load the engine reports the parse error as the held game's stack until the game next stops, so the evaluate's answer says so under note, and stack, variables and evaluate are refused until then. For a game the editor plays, the stack still reads true, and only variables and evaluate are refused. The game's error breaks are held off while its evaluate runs, so an error the evaluate raises does not break the game, and the editor's Ignore Error Breaks setting is back once it answers. For a game the editor plays with no runtime addon, the reason reaches only the editor's Debugger panel, so a null there carries a note saying it may be either. The game reports what an expression raises while it is held inside a runtime_invoke call as raised by that call, and the call's answer says so under errorsNote. Only for op evaluate.

frameId.description: variables, evaluate: which frame, from a stack answer. Default the innermost. A frame the stack no longer holds is refused, and a scope whose values did not arrive in time answers variables null and is named under valuesMissing. Only for ops variables, evaluate.

name: debug_state
title: Debugger state
